product: The "−80 / −85 / −86°C" Dirty Iced Latte (الديرتي المُجمَّد / ديرتي −٨٥). A borosilicate or tempered glass is held for 12+ hours in a laboratory-grade ultra-low-temperature (ULT) freezer at −80 to −86°C. It is lifted out with metal tongs by a barista wearing thick cryo gloves. Chilled flavoured milk at roughly 0°C is poured in; the instant it touches the glass wall it flash-freezes into a wall of milk-frost, while the core stays liquid and just above freezing. A hot ristretto/espresso shot is then poured through the middle, where it cuts a dark channel down the white and bleeds into the frozen rim. The drink has a 30–40 second life: it must be drunk in large sips, not stirred, not shaken, and — critically — cannot be packed for takeaway or delivery. The name "dirty" comes from the way the espresso stains the milk, like ink dropped into cream.
origin:
TWO SEPARATE ORIGINS — the drink, and the deep-freeze format. The deck should not conflate them.

1) THE DRINK — Tokyo, 2010, Katsuyuki Tanaka (田中勝幸), Bear Pond Espresso, Shimokitazawa, Setagaya.
Tanaka spent roughly two decades in the United States (training at Counter Culture Coffee and Gimme Coffee, and known in New York as "Angelstain"), returned to Japan and opened Bear Pond Espresso in Shimokitazawa Ichibangai in 2009 (Metropolis Japan; Makers Bible; Toyo Keizai). His signature espresso "Angel Stain" dates to 2009; "Dirty" dates to 2010, followed by his "coffeedust bar" in 2014 (Bear Pond Espresso's own site lists the sequence: Angel Stain 2009 → Dirty 2010 → coffeedust 2014).
Origin anecdote (reported by Perfect Daily Grind, Sept 2024): a local hair-salon owner told Tanaka she had bought an iced latte on the way to work but could not drink it immediately — by her first sip the ice had melted and watered the texture down. That complaint is the design brief for Dirty: cold, ice-free, undiluted. Named for how the espresso "stains" the milk.
Original construction: no ice at all. Cold milk in a mason jar, espresso extracted directly onto the milk, a second layer of milk, then a second extraction — two layers, roughly 80% espresso / 20% milk on top and 80% milk / 20% espresso below. A Japanese contemporaneous blog post from September 2010 (cafe-mania.cocolog-nifty.com) already describes Dirty as evolving and gaining a reputation among New York baristas — this is the strongest independent confirmation of the 2010 date. At Bear Pond only Tanaka himself is permitted to pull the espresso, using what the shop calls the "B.P.E. Original Technique"; the Angel Stain is capped at roughly 10 per day and served only until 1:00pm. This scarcity ritual is itself part of the DNA the modern version inherited.
Spread from Japan: South Korea → Taiwan → China, then Thailand, and from there to trend-setting cafés in Paris, Berlin, New York and (by 2024) Poland (Perfect Daily Grind; wysocki.coffee). Luckin Coffee was the first Chinese chain to put the word "dirty" on a menu at scale.

2) THE DEEP-FREEZE FORMAT — Shanghai, 20 June 2025, 三立方 (Sān Lì Fāng / "Cubic"), 58 Yongkang Road (永康路58号).
This is the actual thing SHABIM would be building. It is NOT Tokyo and it is NOT old — it is fourteen months old as of August 2026. 三立方 opened on 20 June 2025 as the world's first dedicated Dirty specialty store (全球首家Dirty专门店), built in partnership with the German century-old grinder brand Mahlkönig ("磨王" / 迈赫迪). The menu is radical in its narrowness: only Dirty, only three flavours — rum, vanilla bean, cinnamon (朗姆酒 / 香草荚 / 肉桂). No americano. No filter coffee. No ice.
Method as described by the shop manager to Chinese press: every glass is frozen in a dedicated laboratory-grade freezer (专用的实验级冰箱) to −86°C — the "−80" in the name is the marketing round-number, the real set point is −86°C. Staff put on thick gloves and use tongs to lift the glass out, or they get freezer burn. House-blended flavoured milk at 0°C is poured in; the instant it hits the wall it sets into a layer of "milk frost" (奶霜). Warm fresh espresso is poured on top. Optimal window: 30–40 seconds. House rules: no shaking, no stirring, no takeaway. Texture is described in Chinese coverage as "液态冰淇淋" — liquid ice cream. Price ¥26, and the custom glass goes home with the customer.
So the honest line for the deck: the drink was invented in Tokyo in 2010 by Katsuyuki Tanaka; the ultra-low-temperature spectacle that made it a global phenomenon was invented in Shanghai in June 2025 by 三立方. Everyone else — Hong Kong, Singapore, Melbourne, Penang — is a fast-follower of Shanghai, and every one of them credits Shanghai by name.
virality:
A precise, datable chain. This is not "it went viral" — it is a traceable fourteen-month relay across five cities.

PHASE 1 — SHANGHAI IGNITION, 15 JULY 2025 (the detonation event).
三立方 opened 20 June 2025 and was still only three weeks old (开业仅三周) when it broke. On 15 July 2025, after a heavy rainstorm, photographs and videos spread of a queue of people standing outside 58 Yongkang Road under umbrellas in the downpour, and — the detail that made it a national story — at least one customer who had arrived dragging a wheeled suitcase to carry multiple cups home. The imagery is what went viral, not the coffee: people getting soaked for a drink with a 40-second lifespan.
Platform mechanics: a wave of check-in notes (打卡笔记) and videos on Xiaohongshu (小红书) and Douyin (抖音) fermented rapidly and pushed it onto the trending/hot-search lists (热搜), triggering successive waves of copycat check-ins (Sina Finance, 16 July 2025; Yangcheng Evening News). Chinese commentators explicitly framed the queue itself as a social-media ritual — consumers were queuing to be seen queuing, converting the wait into "traffic capital" (流量资本). Sina Finance ran the piece under the headline "'零下80度咖啡'火出圈，是热爱还是从众？" ("Is it love or herd behaviour?").
Named coverage on that 48-hour spike: Tencent News (15 July 2025), NetEase/163 (15–16 July), Sohu, Sina Finance (16 July), Yangcheng Evening News, Shenzhen News (17 July), Sin Chew Daily Malaysia (15 July), HK01, BusinessFocus Hong Kong, UDN Taiwan, 36Kr (13 July, "把咖啡倒进−86℃冰杯，上海神奇小店爆火，引发全国跟风" — "pour coffee into a −86°C ice cup: a magic little Shanghai shop explodes, triggering nationwide copying"). A medical-desk story ran in parallel — "will drinking it give you frostbite?" — with a doctor quoted saying the risk is lower than it looks because the liquid handed over is above 0°C. Being fact-checked by doctors is itself a virality marker.
Commercial result: from 500 cups a day on weekdays to 800 on public holidays. The manager said they had gone through several rounds of freezers (冰箱换了好几轮) because demand kept outrunning the equipment. Within under a month of opening it hit No.1 on Dianping's Shanghai coffee hot list (大众点评上海咖啡热门榜Top1). People queued 50 minutes in 40°C heat.

PHASE 2 — NATIONWIDE COPYING IN CHINA, JULY–AUTUMN 2025.
36Kr documented the copy wave and, usefully for pricing strategy, the price ladder that emerged: Shanghai 三立方 ¥26 with a custom glass included; Hainan "Plan O Coffee" ¥30 with no glass; Chengdu "川纳万海Daily" ¥40; Beijing "Basepoint咖啡" ¥48. The same drink nearly doubled in price as it travelled 1,200km north. That is the clearest evidence available that this product carries premium-pricing elasticity in a new market.

PHASE 3 — HONG KONG, 19 SEPTEMBER 2025. Ice Bean Cafe launched its −86°C dirty coffee at Shop 7, G/F, Yick Fat Building, 1048 King's Road, Quarry Bay — inside the "Monster Building", already one of Hong Kong's most photographed locations (afoodieworld.com, 19 Sept 2025). Their spec adds a number the Shanghai coverage omits: the cup is chilled for 12+ hours before service, and the window is 30–40 seconds.

PHASE 4 — SINGAPORE, NOVEMBER 2025. Slow Boat, Singapore's first vinyl listening café in Tanjong Pagar, brought the −86°C version in (chueonit.com, 10 November 2025). Hard-capped at 100 cups daily. Three variants: Original, Baileys, Chocolate — the Chocolate sold out in under an hour on its first weekend. Price S$9.80–10, and you keep the glass. Reported wait times exceeded two hours; one documented Lemon8 account queued 10:50am–12:30pm (1h40m) for a single cup. Copycats followed fast in the same city: a −86°C stand (@minus86coolcoffee) outside The Providore at Raffles Place, and Basq & Bean in Bugis doing Milo Dinosaur and Strawberry versions.

PHASE 5 — MELBOURNE, DECEMBER 2025 → JANUARY 2026 (the Western breakout, and the best-documented unit economics anywhere).
Regulars, Ground Floor 38–40 Little La Trobe Street, Melbourne CBD, opened December 2025 — "just after Christmas" — run by husband-and-wife Eddy and Prem Pan. Eddy Pan spent seven years as head roaster at St Ali and is a certified Q Grader; he roasts the beans at his own Balwyn roastery, Roller. Prem came from Tori's. The shop has 16 seats.
Their build refines the Shanghai process into something operationally sharper: the glass gets TWO freezer blasts — first −20°C specifically to prevent thermal shock, then −85°C. Tongs to lift it. Half-filled with full-cream St David Dairy milk. Finished with a ristretto. It is served on a small wooden tray with a printed instruction card: "Sip first, stir later."
Broadsheet published "The Viral Dirty −85°C Coffee Taking Over Melbourne" on 16 January 2026 — three to four weeks after opening. At that point Regulars was selling upwards of 600 glasses a day at A$9 a cup, out of a 16-seat shop, with a queue down the block in "rain, hail or shine" and roughly a 15-minute wait. Broadsheet ran a second piece, "The Viral Dirty Coffee at This Hot Listed Cafe Is Anything but Regular," plus a full venue review, "Regulars, Where Dirty Coffee Is Chilled to −85°C (It's Good)". BeanScene, Australia's coffee trade magazine, called Shanghai Dirty Coffee "the first coffee trend of 2026". Sitchu listed it in "Best Viral Drinks in Melbourne to Try in 2026", noting it "draws queues and sells out fast".
600 glasses/day × A$9 ≈ A$5,400/day from one SKU in a 16-seat room. That is the single most quotable number in this entire research file.

PHASE 6 — STILL RISING, MID-2026. This has not peaked. N.419 Senses Coffee, 419 Lebuh Chulia, George Town, Penang was covered by DanielFoodDiary on 17 June 2026 running −86°C Dirty in Pistachio and Black Sesame — billed as Penang's first. Gulf News ran "Why dirty drinks are the coolest thing on UAE café menus right now" on 18 July 2026, and Curly Tales ran "10 UAE Cafes Serving The Internet's Favourite Viral Dirty Drinks" — but both cover the ordinary layered dirty drink, NOT the ULT-freezer version. Flavour extension is the current growth vector everywhere: Pistamatcha Dirty at Regulars, pistachio and walnut bases, black sesame in Penang, Baileys and chocolate in Singapore.

THE GULF WHITE SPACE — the strategic conclusion. Across every search run in English, Arabic and Chinese, the layered "dirty" drink is confirmed present in the UAE (Typica Café, Between Two Palms, The Grey, Backyard, Glitch Speciality Café, Drinkit) and trending as of July 2026. The −80/−86°C ultra-low-temperature version is NOT confirmed anywhere in the Gulf. Baghdad and the Gulf are open ground for the format that is currently generating two-hour queues in Singapore and 600 cups a day in Melbourne. And the Gulf has an advantage no other market has: at 45–50°C ambient, the thermal contrast — the single thing this product sells — is more violent and more valuable than it is anywhere it has succeeded so far.

ON SOCIAL VIEW COUNTS — AN HONEST LIMIT. TikTok, Instagram and third-party hashtag trackers are all blocked by this environment's egress proxy, and no news outlet in any of the five languages searched published a hashtag aggregate for #dirtycoffee, #dirtylatte or #脏咖啡. I did not find a single credible published total, so I am not inventing one. What IS sourced: one #dirtycoffee TikTok (@semlidut) carrying 148.6K likes and 456 comments; a @penangfoodie −86°C Dirty Latte TikTok at 6,958 likes; and named viral posts including @food.and.grace (tiktok.com/@food.and.grace/video/7589534581976583442) and Instagram reels DS4ekohEZP9, DSzaSolj-wu ("Shanghai's most VIRAL −85C dirty coffee in MELBOURNE"), DVfBFTgEhJS and DXOR_JXEdlS ("Shanghai's viral coffee trend: −80°C Dirty"). Treat every hashtag-scale figure in the deck as an estimate and label it as such.

hard_to_copy:
Nine structural barriers. The important insight is that this product's moat is PHYSICS AND LOGISTICS, not recipe — the recipe is three ingredients and is published everywhere. Nobody can copy it from a photograph, which is exactly why it survived fourteen months of being photographed millions of times.

1. THE COLD IS INVENTORY, NOT A PROCESS STEP. This is the single most important and least obvious barrier. Each glass must sit at −86°C for 12+ hours before it can be sold (Ice Bean Cafe HK). You therefore cannot make a glass on demand. Your maximum daily sales equal the number of glasses physically inside your ULT freezers overnight — not your barista's speed, not your espresso machine, not your queue. To do Regulars' 600 glasses a day you must be storing roughly 600 glasses at −86°C every night. A competitor who buys one freezer has bought a ceiling, not a business. Scaling requires buying cold volume in advance, in cash, before a single cup is sold.

2. LABORATORY-GRADE CAPEX WITH NO SECONDARY USE. A −86°C ULT freezer is medical/research equipment: roughly US$2,700–10,300 for small and mid units, US$25,000+ for large-capacity (American Laboratory Trading, Arctiko, Labrepco, K2 Scientific). Chinese operators reported total outlay of 几十万 RMB — several hundred thousand yuan, roughly US$40k–140k — for freezing equipment plus custom glassware (36Kr). This is not a machine a café already owns, cannot be leased from a coffee supplier, and has zero resale value into the F&B trade. 三立方 went through several rounds of freezers as demand grew (店长: 冰箱换了好几轮) — meaning the capex is not even one-time.

3. THE GLASS IS CUSTOM AND THE FAILURE MODE IS SHATTERING. Ordinary glassware does not survive −86°C, and it certainly does not survive −86°C followed by a hot espresso. Operators use custom cold-resistant tempered/borosilicate vessels (定制耐低温玻璃杯). This is a bespoke supply chain with lead times and minimum orders — a genuine barrier in Iraq and the Gulf, and a genuine advantage once locked with an exclusive supplier.

4. PROCESS IP THAT IS INVISIBLE IN THE VIDEO. Regulars' two-stage protocol — −20°C first specifically to prevent thermal shock, THEN −85°C — is the difference between a working service and a bin full of broken glass. No customer video shows this step, because it happens hours before opening. A copycat watching TikTok will skip it and break their stock.

5. IT CANNOT BE DELIVERED. THIS IS THE MOAT. The 三立方 manager states plainly that if you pack it to go, it is no different from an ordinary latte (若打包跟普通拿铁无异), and the shop refuses takeaway, shaking and stirring outright. The 30–40 second window means Talabat, Deliveroo, Careem, HungerStation and Jahez structurally cannot carry this product. In a Gulf market where delivery aggregators commoditise every café menu and take 25–30% of the ticket, a drink that physically cannot be aggregated is a rare thing: it forces the customer into your room, it keeps 100% of the ticket, and it converts the queue into free advertising. The constraint IS the strategy.

6. THE 40-SECOND WINDOW MANUFACTURES URGENCY AND CONTENT SIMULTANEOUSLY. The product is only beautiful for 40 seconds. That makes filming compulsory — you cannot show a friend, you can only show a video — and it makes the visit non-substitutable. Every customer becomes a distributor. This is why the trend has not decayed in fourteen months across five countries.

7. HANDLING AND SAFETY DISCIPLINE. Staff need thick cryo gloves and metal tongs or they get freezer burn; Chinese media ran doctor-led explainers on frostbite risk. That means trained staff, written SOPs, and a real answer for municipal health inspectors — in Baghdad and the GCC, prepare that dossier BEFORE launch, not after the first inspection.

8. SINGLE-SKU ECONOMICS CUT BOTH WAYS. 三立方 sells only Dirty, in three flavours, with no americano and no filter. 36Kr flags the risk honestly: single product, limited margin headroom, long payback. But it also produces the sharpest brand in the category and the highest throughput per square metre — 600 cups/day out of 16 seats. SHABIM should adopt the narrow menu deliberately, and mitigate with flavour extension, which is exactly what the market is already doing: Pistamatcha and pistachio/walnut bases (Melbourne), black sesame and pistachio (Penang), Baileys and chocolate (Singapore), rum/vanilla/cinnamon (Shanghai).

9. THE GLASS GOES HOME — AND SO DOES THE BRAND. 三立方 and Slow Boat both let the customer keep the custom glass, priced into the ¥26 / S$9.80 ticket. It converts a consumable into a branded object sitting in the customer's kitchen. It also means every cup carries a physical COGS item, so the glass supply contract is simultaneously your marketing budget and your biggest variable cost.

THE GULF-SPECIFIC ADVANTAGE. The one thing this drink sells is thermal contrast, and thermal contrast is worth more the hotter it is outside. Shanghai queued 50 minutes in 40°C. Baghdad and the Gulf run 45–50°C for four months of the year. No market on earth has a stronger natural demand curve for this product than the one SHABIM is entering — and as of August 2026 no ULT-freezer dirty latte is confirmed operating anywhere in the Gulf. Caveat to plan for: the same heat makes the cold chain harder and the electrical load heavier, so specify freezer capacity and backup power for peak-summer ambient, not for spec-sheet conditions.
